children.author: rafram
children.text:
No, the opposite. Firefox WebExtensions inherit the two main security features that XUL extensions used to separate page content from extension code. But in the XUL extension days, if page content did manage to control an extension, it could directly take over your machine and execute any code with full filesystem access.

(The two security features are X-ray vision and cross-origin access controls. The former makes it so extension code doesn’t see the page’s modifications to built-in properties. For example, if my extension calls document.createRange(), but the page has overwritten that method, my code will see the original and not the modified version. But if I call document.wrappedJSObject.createRange(), I ask to get the page’s version, which might be malicious. The latter just means that objects created by extensions and made accessible to the page can’t actually be used by it unless the extension explicitly exports them. Both of these are still active for WebExtensions.)

Lotta rose-tinted glasses when people remember the XUL extension days. It was an extraordinarily risky and fragile architecture. Every single extension had full control over your machine, and every major Firefox update broke most extensions (or made them break Firefox), because the main way to inject your logic into the browser was monkey-patching.

That doesn't really answer the question. Sure, XUL extensions have better access to the internals of the browser. But does that translate into XUL extensions being able to better isolate their own internals from being accessed by untrusted websites?

A browser should not be concerned with the interests of commercial players. Software should, first and foremost, take the interests of users into account.
If they try to do something against Firefox, we have to fight back. Just going along with it and giving in will only lead, in the long run, to the Internet becoming even more broken than it already is.

That's an argument in favor of extensions. Most of the examples you listed are features that oppose the interests of most commercial players on the market, including but not limited to, many multinational corporations. If they were all first-party features of the browser, Firefox would've been dead a long time ago.

As it is, they're just voluntary extra software that Firefox neither bundles nor recommends explicitly, which keeps both the browsers and extensions safe - merely supporting arbitrary extensions in general is not enough to create focused market pushback against the browser (and gives Fx some leverage, mostly around "accessibility"), while individual extensions are too small a target to fight.

It's a good separation of concerns, and a somewhat stable equilibrium.

The solution would be to properly implement the features that enough users want into the browser. After all, extensions are usually just a stopgap measure. Firefox could also simply build in an ad blocker that works just as well as uBlock Origin. For password managers, they could simply build an API into the browser that password managers could then use to integrate with the browser. Then there would be no need for an extra extension. The same goes for things like add-ons to download videos from sites that prevent it, such as YouTube or similar streaming sites. If Firefox simply had a built-in feature to scrape video files from websites and save them normally via the right-click menu, no one would install dubious extensions for that purpose.

The concept of browser extensions seems terrible in general. There are many that ship with malware, botnets, infostealers etc. uBlock Origin even requires a compiled .wasm module. It's unwise to grant that level of complexity from third party devs permission over something as sensitive as your web browser.

children.text:
The entire point of browser extensions is to operate outside the default sandbox. They're browser extensions, not browser content extensions.

On one hand we're widening what a tab may do, throwing dozens of permission prompts at users until they're fatigued, on the other we're trying to lock down extensions to the point of making them redundant. I wouldn't be surprised if by the time manifest v5 rolls around, tabs and extensions will be indistinguishable.

At that point someone will create a chrome mod "SuperExtensions", sourcing extensions from a third-party marketplace that is worse and less secure in every way than what we had in 2020, but at least gives people control over the software that runs on their hardware with actually useful exensions again. Such as adblock that doesn't suck. Or an extension that neuters spyware built into browsers.

But of course it wasn't about those extensions at all. It was all about security, not Alphabet's bottom line. Because we can trust people to vote, drive, drink, and do plenty of things, but we can't trust them to decide what software runs on their computer. The paternalistic security argument of the technological infant. Honi soit qui mal y pense.

Edit: Sorry for the only tangentially related rant.

children.text: You see, the company behind the most used browser isn't motivated by this.

That sounds like a halving of performance for marginal security gain, when we have such glaring holes like extensions having unfettered access to all network requests made by the browser (the gap that manifest v3 moved towards closing).
Browsers should implement something like a sandboxed DOM where execution is limited to a snapshot of the DOM. This would prevent most of the client side related vulnerabilities.
